newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY GDP RISE COULD WIDEN TRADE GAP - BANK REPORT.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY GDP RISE COULD WIDEN TRADE GAP - BANK REPORT.

text.p: Hungary's gross domestic product (GDP) will grow by up to three percent this year, but increasing imports could recreate tension in the foreign trade balance, Budapest Bank analysts said on Thursday.

General Electric-controlled Budapest Bank (BB) said in its regular spring economic forecast that Hungary's two year old economic stabilisation programme had created the foundation of growth but had not eliminated all tensions in the economy.
"We expect moderate growth in 1999, with maintained structural tension," BB chief analyst Peter Bihari told a news conference.
BB forecasts household consumption to recover this year and rise by 0.5 to one percent, after an about 10 percent fall in 1995 and 1996.

As the economy has been cooled by a shrinking domestic market, enterprises in Hungary are very sensitive to even slight changes in domestic consumption and an improving outlook is likely to encourage them to boost investments, Bihari said.
As a result, investments will grow by six to eight percent in 1997, compared to a preliminary statistical office 1996 figure of a 4.4 percent decline.
With government investments growing by some 40 percent in 1997, increased domestic economic activity will boost GDP by 1.5 to three percent in 1997, compared with some 0.5 percent in 1996, BB said.

BB and the think-tank GKI, which published its 1997 forecast on Wednesday, both maintain that the main risk in the expected stimulation of the economy was a larger inflow of foreign goods, threatening a soaring trade deficit.
GKI said the trade gap was likely to widen by $400 to 500 million this year, while Bihari projected an increase of $600 to $700 million to levels between $3.1 and $3.3 billion.

However, an almost eight percent decrease in customs duties this year, a growth in GDP and potentially rising import demand by industry, may even boost the trade gap to above $3.5 billion, which is already near the levels which forced Hungary to launch a strict austerity programme in 1995, Bihari added.

If all these factors have a more negative than expected impact on the trade balance, the government will have to introduce special measures in 1998 which could including a quicker forint devaluation, Bihari said.

GKI and BB agree that the National Bank of Hungary should continue its efforts to stabilise the current interest rate levels to prevent real yields turning negative as that could trigger a flight of capital from the country.

They also agree that inflation was likely to reverse a one-year declining trend in the next six months and rise slightly on the regular quarterly energy price adjustments and larger food prices increases, which were relatively moderate last year.

BB expects average inflation to drop to 19 to 19.5 percent from 23.6 percent last year, while year-on-year CPI in December will be about the same level, slightly below 20 percent, than in December 1996, BB said.
